questions.q: In simple harmonic motion the acceleration is:
options: Proportional to the displacement and in the same direction
Proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction
questions.solution:
SHM is **defined** by $a = -\omega^{2}x$.

The acceleration is proportional to the displacement and **directed opposite to it** — always back towards the mean position, which is what makes the motion oscillate.

The acceleration is maximum at the extremes and zero at the centre; the velocity is the other way round.

questions.q: The period of a simple pendulum of length $L$ is:
questions.solution:
$T = \mathbf{2\pi\sqrt{L/g}}$, for small oscillations.

The mass of the bob does not appear — a heavy pendulum and a light one of the same length swing at the same rate. Quadrupling the length doubles the period.

questions.q: The relation between wave speed, frequency and wavelength is:
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{v = f\lambda}$.

In one period the wave advances exactly one wavelength, and there are $f$ periods per second.

For a given medium $v$ is fixed, so frequency and wavelength are inversely related — a higher-pitched sound has a shorter wavelength.

questions.q: In SHM the total energy is proportional to:
questions.solution:
$E = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^{2}A^{2}$, so $E \propto \mathbf{A^{2}}$.

Doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy. The total is constant throughout the motion, exchanging between kinetic and potential twice each cycle.

questions.q: A source of sound approaches a stationary observer. The observed frequency is:
questions.solution:
For an approaching source the wavefronts pile up, so the observed frequency is **higher**:

$f' = f\left(\dfrac{v}{v - v_s}\right)$

This is the drop in pitch you hear as an ambulance passes: high on approach, low as it recedes. Note the **speed** of sound itself is unchanged — only the wavelength and frequency shift.

questions.q: A mass $m$ on a spring of stiffness $k$ oscillates with angular frequency:
questions.solution:
$F = -kx = ma$ gives $a = -\dfrac{k}{m}x$, and comparing with $a = -\omega^{2}x$:

$\omega = \mathbf{\sqrt{k/m}}$, so $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.

Unlike the pendulum, this one **does** depend on the mass, and it works the same in zero gravity.

questions.q: The fundamental frequency of a string of length $L$ fixed at both ends, carrying waves of speed $v$, is:
questions.solution:
Both ends are fixed, so both are nodes. The fundamental has one antinode in the middle, which means $L = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$, so $\lambda = 2L$.

$f_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \mathbf{\dfrac{v}{2L}}$.

The harmonics are $nv/2L$ — all integer multiples, which is why a string sounds musical. A pipe closed at one end gives $v/4L$ and only the odd harmonics.

questions.q: Two tuning forks of frequencies $256\ \text{Hz}$ and $260\ \text{Hz}$ are sounded together. The beat frequency is:
questions.solution:
The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies:

$f_b = |f_1 - f_2| = |260 - 256| = \mathbf{4\ \text{Hz}}$.

Four loudness maxima are heard per second — this is exactly how an instrument is tuned by ear, by adjusting until the beats disappear.

In a gas the particles oscillate **along** the direction of travel, producing compressions and rarefactions — the wave is **longitudinal**.

A gas has no shear rigidity, so it cannot carry a transverse mechanical wave at all. That is why transverse waves are a diagnostic for a solid, and why S-waves from an earthquake do not cross the Earth's liquid outer core.

questions.q: A pendulum has a period of $2\ \text{s}$. What is its period, in seconds, if its length is quadrupled?
A wave of frequency $500\ \text{Hz}$ has a wavelength of $0.68\ \text{m}$. Find its speed, in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
questions.solution: $v = f\lambda = 500 \times 0.68 = \mathbf{340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}$ — the speed of sound in air at room temperature.

questions.q: A particle in SHM has amplitude $5\ \text{cm}$ and angular frequency $4\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$. Find its maximum speed, in $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}$.
questions.solution:
The speed is greatest at the mean position, where

$v_{\max} = \omega A = 4 \times 5 = \mathbf{20\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}}$.

For comparison, the maximum acceleration is $\omega^{2}A = 80\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-2}}$, and occurs at the extremes.

questions.q: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass on a spring of stiffness $200\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ oscillates. Find the angular frequency, in $\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
A string of length $0.5\ \text{m}$ carries waves at $100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and is fixed at both ends. Find its fundamental frequency, in hertz.

Show that a simple pendulum executes simple harmonic motion for small oscillations, and derive its time period. State clearly where the small-angle approximation enters and why the result fails for large amplitudes.
questions.solution:
**Setting up.** A bob of mass $m$ hangs on a light inextensible string of length $L$. Displace it so the string makes an angle $\theta$ with the vertical.

Two forces act: the weight $mg$ downwards and the tension $T$ along the string.

**Resolving.** Along the string, the tension is balanced by $mg\cos\theta$ and the net centripetal requirement — it does no work and produces no torque about the pivot.

Perpendicular to the string (tangential to the arc), the restoring force is

$F = -mg\sin\theta$

The minus sign says it acts back towards the vertical.

**In terms of displacement.** The arc displacement from the mean position is $x = L\theta$, so $\theta = x/L$.

$F = -mg\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{L}\right)$

**The small-angle approximation.** This is **not** yet SHM, because $\sin\theta$ is not proportional to $\theta$. For small $\theta$ (in radians),

$\sin\theta \approx \theta$

This is where the approximation enters, and it is the **only** step that is not exact. Then

$F \approx -\dfrac{mg}{L}x$

**This is SHM.** The force is proportional to the displacement and opposite in direction, which is the definition. Comparing with $F = -m\omega^{2}x$:

$m\omega^{2} = \dfrac{mg}{L} \Rightarrow \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{g}{L}}$

**The period.**

$T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \boxed{2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}}$

The mass has cancelled, so the period is independent of the bob — Galileo's observation.

**Why it fails at large amplitude.** The true equation is $\ddot\theta = -\dfrac{g}{L}\sin\theta$, and $\sin\theta < \theta$ for $\theta > 0$. So the real restoring force is **weaker** than the linear approximation predicts, and the pendulum takes **longer** than $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.

The first correction is

$T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\left(1 + \dfrac{\theta_0^{2}}{16}\right)$

At $\theta_0 = 10^\circ$ ($0.175$ rad) the error is about $0.2\%$ — negligible. At $60^\circ$ it is around $7\%$, which is why a pendulum clock is built to swing through only a few degrees.

The motion is still periodic at large amplitude, but it is no longer **simple harmonic**: the period now depends on the amplitude, which SHM never does.
